400: I ask everyone the same question all day: anything to declare? Almost everyone says no. Almost everyone is wrong.
401: My whole job is one question. You would think people would practice the answer before they reach my desk.
402: Someone once said no, then remembered a live turtle in their coat. We both took a quiet moment.
403: People forget the strangest things. A whole cheese. A second suitcase. Once, a small tree.
404: I ask what you are carrying. The honest ones list three things. The bag, if asked, would list nine.
405: A man told me he had nothing to declare, then his bag began to hum. I still think about that bag.
406: I have heard every version of nothing. Some of them weigh forty pounds.
407: My favorite moment is when a perfectly calm face suddenly remembers the one thing it hoped I would not ask about.
408: You declare nothing. I nod. Then I open the bag and we both learn something new.
409: I spend my days sorting the honest travelers from the optimistic ones. Usually they turn out to be the same traveler.
410: People pack their whole life into a bag, then swear the bag is empty. I admire the confidence.
411: Anything to declare, I ask. They pause. That pause tells me more than any answer ever could.
412: Once a traveler declared a sandwich. Just one sandwich. Honestly, it was refreshing.
413: The job is simple: ask, wait, believe nothing, and smile the whole time anyway.
414: I have watched grown adults forget an entire second coat they were, at that moment, wearing.
415: Every day I learn what people think does not count. It is usually the biggest item in the bag.
416: A woman said no, then produced eleven jars of jam from a coat clearly designed for holding jam.
417: I ask, they answer, and somewhere at their feet a suitcase quietly disagrees with all of it.
418: This job trained me to notice the one bag a person is trying very hard not to look at.
419: People declare the boring things and forget the interesting ones. To be fair, so would I.
420: I lift boxes all day. I do not know what is inside them. I stopped wondering a long time ago.
421: My back has opinions now. It shares them every morning, loudly, before I have even stood up.
422: I carried a crate today that weighed more than I do. We did not part as friends.
423: People ask what I do. I move heavy things from one place to a slightly less convenient place.
424: Every crate looks the same until you lift it. Then it becomes a very personal experience.
425: Once a huge crate turned out to be completely empty. I have never felt more personally betrayed by a box.
426: The dock has one rule: if it is heavy, it belongs to me. Everything here is heavy.
427: I moved forty crates before lunch. Then lunch arrived, and it was also heavy, so I moved that too.
428: You grow strong doing this. You also grow very good at not thinking about your knees.
429: A crate today was marked fragile. It weighed as much as a small horse. I was gentle anyway.
430: My whole life is picking up one heavy thing and setting it down near another heavy thing.
431: I do not ask what is in the boxes. Curiosity has never once helped me lift one.
432: Some days the crates win. You set them down, nod at them, and agree to try again tomorrow.
433: I have strong arms and a short memory. Both are absolutely required for this job.
434: The heaviest crate always sits at the very bottom. I suspect the dock was designed by someone who dislikes me.
435: I stacked boxes taller than my own house. Then someone told me they go on a different boat.
436: People think it is all muscle. It is mostly patience, and a little quiet complaining under my breath.
437: I carried something so heavy today that I briefly forgot my own name. It was a peaceful moment.
438: The crates never say thank you. Years ago, I stopped waiting for them to start.
439: Lift it, carry it, set it down, do it again. My shoulders keep a very detailed record of every single one.
